The dispensed costs under the 2-MTPD scenarios, as well as all other station capacity scenarios, are lowest at high station utilization ($6.50/kg - $7.70/kg) but are above the threshold price of $4/kg - $5/kg. Government support and/or rapid technology learning and adoption would be necessary to reduce costs to threshold values. Note that the production cost of $1.50/kg H in 2 Figure 45 is based on incumbent production pathways (i.e., SMR), but maturing production pathways, such as renewable electrolysis, may reach similar cost in some locations if tax credits from the Inflation Reduction Act are leveraged (Bracci, Koleva, and Chung 2024; DOE 2024). 84 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 45. Potential total levelized cost of hydrogen dispensed under various heavy-duty refueling station capacity and lifetime utilization rate assumptions. See Bracci, Koleva, and Chung (2024) for more detail. The dispensed levelized cost of hydrogen values do not include additional markup or incentives that could affect the price of hydrogen fuel to the customer. In California, the Alliance for Clean Hydrogen Energy Systems (ARCHES) hydrogen hub estimates about 11 MTPD of hydrogen demand for direct use in aircraft by 2035, spread out over eight in-state airports (Chen et al. 2025). This results in an average of 1.4 MTPD of demand per airport in 2035, with dispensed costs of hydrogen most likely to align with those presented under the 2-MTPD scenarios in Figure 45. By 2045, ARCHES estimates direct hydrogen-powered aviation could have a total demand over 200 MTPD spread out over the major airports in the state of California. This would yield dispensed costs in line with the 4-, 8-, and 18-MTPD sections of Figure 45, as average airport demands will have grown higher than the 2035 average of 1.4 MTPD (Bracci, Koleva, and Chung 2024; Chen et al. 2025). As mentioned in Section 4.1.22.2, liquid hydrogen tanker trucking, which is assumed in Figure 45, is the most viable delivery option to airports with throughput on the order of 1 MTPD – 10 MTPD, similar to this California example. Once airport hydrogen demand exceeds this threshold, hydrogen pipeline delivery or on-site liquid hydrogen production become more realistic options. This is because (1) multiple liquid truck hydrogen deliveries per day can lead to traffic congestion and other logistical difficulties at the airport, and (2) better economies of scale are achieved for pipelines and on-site LH production at higher demand levels. With this in mind, and with demand 2 estimates from ARCHES, it is realistic that liquid hydrogen tanker trucks can be the primary mode of delivery to airports in California until midcentury, with on-site production or pipeline pathways becoming more economically viable afterward. 85 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications.
